title_zh: 西奥多·贝扎是谁？
content:
Theodore Beza is an unfamiliar figure today in the evangelical world. He has been much maligned by many historians and theologians who created the image of an austere man who turned Calvin’s theology into an arid scholastic system. This image is actually very far from the truth. So who was Theodore Beza really?
He was born in Vézelay, France, in 1519 in an affluent family of the minor French nobility. His life spanned almost the whole sixteenth century, and he died in 1605 at the age of eighty-six. By God’s providence, there were two clear turning points in his life.
The first occurred at the age of nine when he was placed as a lodger with a Lutheran scholar, Melchior Wolmar, who became his preceptor. He spent seven years with Wolmar, who taught him law, Latin, and Greek. Interestingly, one of Wolmar’s other students during that time was none other than Calvin, who was just ten years older than Beza. Wolmar gave Beza a first-rate education, and, like Calvin, Beza was likely more fluent in Latin than in French. More importantly, Wolmar was instrumental in his journey toward the new Reformed faith. It was through Wolmar that, sometime around 1535, Beza read a book by the Swiss Reformer Heinrich Bullinger and was converted. Years later, Beza wrote to Bullinger: “You made known to me true piety, and its purest source: The Word of God.”
1
However, Beza had a lot to lose if he disclosed his newfound faith. He received substantial ecclesiastical incomes through one of his uncles, who was an abbot, and this allowed him to enjoy a life of pleasure in Paris, dedicating himself to poetry and humanistic studies. For several years, he kept his faith secret, and he secretly married Claudine Denosse, the daughter of a Parisian Protestant merchant. Beza promised he would marry her publicly whenever they could find a truly Reformed church.
The second turning point of his life came in 1548 when he contracted the plague and came close to death. He took it as a clear warning from God and came out openly about his faith. Shortly after, he fled to Geneva. Theodore and Claudine were publicly married by Calvin himself, and they remained devoted to each other and to the cause of Christ until Claudine’s death in 1588.
After teaching Greek in Lausanne for a few years, Beza settled in Geneva permanently in 1558, mainly because of his admiration for Calvin. He lived there until his death, faithfully serving alongside Calvin and assuming his mantle as leader of the French Reformed church after Calvin’s death in 1564.
Beza’s legacy is immense and multifaceted, and it is difficult to summarize it in a few words. He was first and foremost a man of letters. One of his first tasks in Geneva was to complete the translation of the Psalms from Hebrew into French for the Huguenot psalter, a translation left unfinished by another Reformed poet at his death. Beza also published a critical edition of the Greek New Testament that was influential on the Textus Receptus, from which the King James Bible was translated. In fact, the 1565 edition was dedicated to Queen Elizabeth I. In many ways, this was Beza’s lifetime project. He tirelessly corrected and improved the text and published several editions, with the last major revision appearing in 1598. In 1559, he published a “Confession of the Christian Faith,” addressed to his father, to explain why he had embraced the Reformed faith. Although it was penned in a few days, it was hugely popular, as it was published at least thirty-five times during his lifetime and translated into Latin, English, German, and Dutch.
He consolidated Calvin’s legacy in Geneva by preaching regularly and teaching theology for forty years. We know from several sources that his teaching was greatly appreciated. For example, an alumnus wrote in 1578:
We listened to you with so much admiration and pleasure. Apart from your own personality traits, you combined Melanchthon’s penetrating insights, Calvin’s solid and direct common sense, and Vermigli’s

content:
What was the matter with the Protestant Reformation? It might seem like a strange question. Some might say that there was nothing the matter with the Reformation, that it was the acme of spiritual recovery of biblical Christianity in church history and therefore was a sort of golden age of biblical faith. Others might say that the matter with the Reformation was that there was one at all, since it produced the largest schism in church history.
That’s not what I mean, however, when I ask about what was the matter with the Protestant Reformation. I’m not using the word matter in the normal way, which typically indicates that something is wrong. When we ask, “What’s the matter with you?” we are assuming that something is wrong or that we’re looking for fault. What I mean, by contrast, is this: What was the essence, the substance, or what is called in philosophy the
material cause
of the Protestant Reformation? Another way to ask it would be this: What was the chief issue that provoked such massive consequences as this split that occurred in the sixteenth century?
When historians consider the causes of the Protestant Reformation, they often use distinctions originally set forth by the philosopher Aristotle, and they distinguish between the
formal cause
and the
material cause
. The formal cause, the intellectual background to the issue, was a dispute over the seat of final authority that binds the Christian conscience. We’ll look at that under the heading of
sola Scriptura
. The
material cause
, however, the substantive issue that was the core point of dispute, was the doctrine of justification. The Protestant view of this matter is expressed in the shorthand of the Latin phrase
sola fide
.
This is the first of the Latin slogans of the Reformation known as the five
solas
. They are
sola fide
, justification is by faith alone;
sola gratia
, salvation is by grace alone;
solus Christus
, salvation is through Christ alone;
sola Scriptura
, the sole authority that binds the conscience of the Christian is the Bible alone; and then, finally,
soli Deo gloria
, to God alone belongs the glory.
Sola fide
is shorthand for the central issue of the Reformation, the material cause, which was the question of justification. The Protestant Reformers set forth a doctrine that our justification is by faith and by faith alone without any mixture of good works or merit on our part.
To understand
sola fide
in its historical context, we have to understand something about the theological dispute based on the Roman Catholic understanding of justification. At the heart of this dispute was not a tangential debate over how many angels can dance on the head of a pin or a needless controversy over pedantic points of theology that only academics care about. Rather, this issue touched the very heart of the Christian faith because the question of justification is designed to answer this deeper question: How can an unjust person possibly survive the judgment of a just and holy God?
In our day, the doctrine of justification has been degraded in terms of its perceived importance. Historically, the differences among churches over how we obtain a right standing before God were considered significant; those differences have now been minimized as having no great weight. We’re living in a time of relativism, which says that there is no objective truth, and pluralism, which declares that there are many different approaches to truth and views of truth. Therefore, people assert, doctrinal issues should never divide us because what really counts are personal relationships, not doctrine. That notion is propounded even though the New Testament is replete with Apostolic concern about correct doctrine. Sadly, that’s not where the church is in this day and age, and sometimes we have to ask, Why?

Pastors are often asked about how to encourage men to be more involved in the life of the church. For a variety of reasons, the perception among men is that the church is not a place for doing manly things. Unless men take active leadership roles, the involvement of men in the church is often limited to attending a single service on Sunday. The absence of male service in the church is detrimental to the progress and health of the entire body. Perhaps the proverbial question, “Adam, where are you?” continues to be asked most often regarding men serving in the kingdom of God.
There appears to be a significant disconnect for men between certain activities that provide a sense of purpose and accomplishment—such as work, sports, and other recreational activities—and active service the church. Great encouragement is needed for men to view serving in the church as a critical component of their calling in this life. Such service is not merely personally fulfilling, but it builds up and strengthens the entire body of Christ. There is nothing more Christlike than a man laying down his life for his friends. This, according to Jesus, is true greatness.
There are many ways to encourage men to serve in the church. Sometimes, however, we think too highly about this question. It’s always important to begin with those things that seem insignificant to us. One does not have to be an ordained office bearer to do great works among us. In a word: Think smaller. It is in the little things that great things are achieved, even if it is taking a cup of cold water to someone in need. With these things in mind, what follows are five simple encouragements for men regarding how they might serve well in the local church.
1. Pursue growth in the Scriptures.
First and most important is the personal growth of the man himself. A great servant is not created by merely doing. It begins with the mind and the heart. A servant is formed, not coerced by guilt. The mind must be renewed by understanding the love of Christ for us, then our love for others becomes properly motivated. Becoming a servant happens by pursuing growth in the Scriptures. Yes, this requires heartfelt attendance to the means of grace in worship on Sunday. This is a top priority. But it also requires the weekly pursuit of our own development spiritually toward the end of helping others grow in the faith. Active involvement in Bible studies and other groups centered around the Word and prayer will help shape us to have the mind of Christ. Growing together with other men in study is an equipping type of service in the body that will result in cultivating fellowship, making us effective in serving the needs of others. Make use of these opportunities for growth.

The result is that men think they do not have the gifts for this high calling and so service in the body is often left to ordained men. This is certainly a wrong view of the basic calling of the Christian man. While the requirements for office bearers are described in passages such as 1 Timothy 3, this does not mean that these qualities should only be pursued by ordained men. All men should think about the use of these gifts even if they do not serve in an official capacity. In general, men ought to aspire to practice them. Opportunities abound such as reading the Scriptures to encourage the afflicted, visiting the sick, helping those in need, and praying for the body. Recognizing that these duties belong to all men is an important first step, then knowing the body and serving them is what follows.

content:
I recently spent a couple of weeks preparing a great deal of fresh material for a weekend-long marriage seminar. Along the way, I often found myself convicted by the content I was preparing. As I readied myself to teach others, I had to consider the ways in which I needed to be a student before I should be a teacher. One area this proved true was intimacy in marriage—but a kind of intimacy I think many of us seldom consider.
There is no doubt that marriage is meant to involve a husband and wife baring their bodies before one another, so that marriage is the context in which a man and woman can experience what it is to be naked and unashamed—to be fully bared, yet fully accepted. And because marriage is meant to be the deepest kind of unity two human beings can experience, it makes sense that there is
a physical component to it
through which two bodies are literally joined together. This is usually what we mean when we discuss intimacy in marriage.
It is my understanding that this kind of intimacy, while real, is also in a way representative or symbolic. It is a demonstration of a unity between two people that is
not merely body-deep
, but fully soul-deep. Physical intimacy is both significant and essential to marriage, but it is not meant to be the sum total of the intimacy shared between a husband and wife. Yet as Aileen and I have interacted with other couples, we have observed that many husbands and wives find it easier to bare their bodies than their souls. Even as they routinely give themselves to one another physically, they can withhold a great deal relationally and emotionally. Even as they give themselves in free and joyful lovemaking, they can stop short of a greater baring, which is the baring of their souls and the revealing of the deep recesses of their hearts.
As Aileen and I discussed this together, we had to conclude that this is something we are prone to as well. It’s not that we hold back shocking secrets or scandalous sins that would cause the other to recoil in dismay or disgust. It’s that we are both reserved people who find it hard to let another person in. We are both wounded people who have been hurt by those who have misused information we have revealed to them. And then I suppose we are both prideful or distrustful people who hold back the pieces of ourselves that we think might cause the other person to lower their respect for us. But by holding back, we are failing to live with full transparency and, therefore, failing to live with full intimacy. The baring of our bodies exceeds the baring of our souls.
There is an irony to this, because I am convinced there is a deep longing within each of us to be known. We want someone else to know us as we truly are and to still love us and give us their approval. But even while we want it on one level, we resist it on another, because we wonder what that other person will think of us if they know our deep thoughts, our secret longings, and our hidden fears. We wonder if they will still respect us if they know what causes us to feel shame or express remorse. Perhaps we doubt they’ll still love us if they know who we are far beneath the surface. Still, there is this longing to be known, to be as bare emotionally as we can be physically—and still to be loved and accepted. It is this longing that we never address when we hold back from revealing who and what we truly are, when we refuse to foster a deep soul intimacy—an intimacy that is then represented by, rather than superseded by, sexual intimacy.
So how can we foster this kind of baring?
By letting our spouse really know us, which may mean creating times and contexts for lengthy, deep, and uninterrupted conversation. This will involve
asking good questions
and then listening attentively so we can come to a correct rather than trite or hasty understanding of what is being communicated. To really know and be known is the work of a lifetime. It is work, but work worth committing to.

This question often arises when we discuss same-sex attraction. Writing for Logos, Mark Jones explores the concept of concupiscence from a Reformed perspective.
In brief, concupiscence (concupiscentia) originates from the Latin verb concupisco, which means ‘to ardently desire.’ There are proper, non-sinful forms of desire, which we would call ‘non-sinful concupiscence.’ For example, Jesus said to his disciples, ‘I have earnestly desired [ἐπεθύμησα] to eat this Passover with you before I suffer’ (Luke 22:15). But because we live in a fallen world, concupiscence typically has in view sinful desire, and usually in reference to sinful sexual desires. Because sin is the privation (lack) of righteousness and proneness to evil, concupiscence involves not just the acts but the desire of the person. Sinful concupiscence can be understood from God’s moral law: ‘You shall not covet’ (Exod 20:17).

Sometimes one word is all that stands between the truth and a lie, between life and death. In the Reformation, that word was

While many people sought to work their way to heaven, the Reformers boldly proclaimed the only true gospel: salvation is by God’s grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, to the glory of God alone.

content:
I can’t quite decide: Has AI already been around long enough that we can say we’re now living in an AI world? Or is AI so new that it has still only made the smallest impact compared to what will be the case five or ten years from now? Regardless, there’s no doubt that AI is here to stay and that we will all need to learn how to live with it. Even if we choose to avoid using it directly, it is going to be a constant presence in the background of our lives as it becomes a core product for businesses, governments, and every other institution we rely on or interact with. In that way, there is no avoiding it.

I would like to think time will prove that Christians are already thinking about AI in
a distinctly Christian way
. Those who use AI widely and those who reject it entirely are both under obligation to think about it well. Thankfully, we are quickly being resourced with helpful books that can guide us. The latest of these is Pete Killingley’s
A Christian’s Guide to AI: 12 Biblical Answers to the Questions We’re All Asking
.
In his book, Killingley does exactly what the subtitle states: he asks a series of questions about AI and then answers them in a distinctly Christian way. His purpose is neither to endorse AI nor to disparage it, but to help readers understand it and, therefore, rightly evaluate it before they integrate it deeply into their lives. Here’s how he introduces this book:
A common view of the church is that we’re always a few years behind the world when it comes to any cultural or technological change. Whether that’s true or not, we should be asking where we want to be as churches: at the forefront of the change or picking up the pieces of the people AI leaves in its wake?
As Christians, we do need to start thinking about AI deliberately. The fact that you’ve picked up this book means you probably agree. It would be so easy for us to split into our camps of tech-lovers and technophobes … and then use or not use AI as we each see fit. Because the Bible doesn’t give us a handbook for how to relate to AI, we would each create our own guidelines, often without a huge amount of thought.
But as I’ve studied AI over the last few years and given seminars on the topic to churches and church leaders, I’ve been struck that although the Bible doesn’t explicitly mention AI, it does give us an abundance of theological themes that help us understand the AI revolution. Whether that be our theology of humanity, of technology, of creativity, of work, of friendship or of the future, the Bible is not silent.
Indeed, it is not.
The book’s first chapter begins with the most basic question of all: What is AI? His definition is simple, and borrowed from David Betts: “a human-made simulation of intelligence in a machine.” Because AI is a mere simulation of intelligence, he suggests we read the acronym as “apparent intelligence” rather than “artificial intelligence”—a surprisingly helpful tweak to the term. He explains the different forms AI takes and singles out large language models as the kind we use most often.
The second question deals with our humanity and asks what makes us different from AI. This leads to a discussion of man being made in the image of God and the necessity of holding a high view of our humanity. The next chapter turns to the nature of truth and explains some of the ways AI can distort the truth: through factual inaccuracies, flattery, and bias.
Further chapters offer hope for those whose jobs may be imperiled by AI and explain whether it is right to use it to create art. It then moves to some of the questions that are probably top of mind for the average reader: Can I have an AI friend? Can I use AI to help me with my essay? Should I use AI to help me write my Bible talk? Should I use AI to make important decisions? Can AI help us share the gospel? Good morning, my friends. Thanks for reading today’s A La Carte. I’m so thankful for the privilege of putting it together day by day, and I’m glad you’re willing to read it. I trust you’ll find something that blesses and encourages you.

Kindle deals

The War on Children
,
The Grace of Giving
).
Recommended Reading
We have 10,000 Digital Guides; We Need Spiritual Fathers.
Zach Hollifield draws a useful comparison between ancient Corinth and today. “You and I live in a digital Corinth, and we too certainly have ‘countless guides in Christ’. Podcasts, social media accounts, YouTube channels, book authors, Xers, Substackers, sermons from celebrity pastors we care for more than the ones coming from the pulpits at our own churches—we have countless guides in Christ. More countless than the Corinthians could have dreamed of.”
You’ll Never Regret That You Did the Right Thing.
I often say “you’ll never regret the sins you don’t commit.” A positive way to express that is what Jacob Crouch communicates here: you’ll never regret doing the right thing. “Let me be the voice in your ear for a minute: Do the right thing. You will never regret that you did.”
Take Your Faith Deeper with Ligonier’s
Grow
App.
We have access to more content than ever before, but how much of it is trustworthy? The
Grow
app from Ligonier Ministries offers carefully curated Bible teaching that has served Christians for decades. In addition to thousands of free resources to read, watch or listen to, Ligonier’s Ministry Partners can also access the notes from the
Reformation Study Bible
and the Ask Ligonier intelligent assistant tool to get reliable answers to pressing theological questions. Not a Ligonier Ministry Partner yet? Try these features for 30 days when you sign in to the app. (Sponsored)
Reformed Doesn’t Mean Robotic: a Case for Expressive Worship.
Thembelani Maqajana writes about coming to Reformed convictions in theology, and then evaluating Reformed worship. “For many Africans, music and movement are naturally connected. Clapping, swaying, raising hands or moving rhythmically communicate joy, thanksgiving, celebration, and participation. We shouldn’t label expressive worship as mere emotionalism. The important question to ask, then, isn’t: ‘are people moving?’; but ‘what is motivating their movement, and is it consistent with biblical worship?'”
The Solitary Grief of Miscarriage.
Luke Fong and his wife recently suffered a miscarriage. He writes about the solitary grief of it, but also encourages Christians to break the solitude by letting others into their sorrow. “Grief must be shared, regardless of whether one feels as though one is imposing on another by doing so. One thing my wife and I have learned, or are learning, through this experience, is that we have to trust that those who are our brothers and sisters in Christ do truly love us. We must trust that love can bear burdens, because love draws us out of our sorrow and into the truth that we are known and bound together in Christ.”
The True Voice of Aslan.
In the context of the forthcoming Narnia movies, Steven West goes to the source, which is to say, to the works of C.S. Lewis, to discover the true voice of Aslan. “Both the vocal and physical characteristics of Aslan are significant and evocative, and they cannot be changed without fundamentally altering his character and Lewis’s intentional symbolism. Aslan’s voice, mane, and other physical features are not window-dressing details—they are an important part of Aslan’s character and significant for the holistic integrity of Lewis’s presentation.”
